confidence_note: Scene widened to the customer-voice thread in Stone's book: speakerphone call + question-mark escalations + empty chair. Sources (secondary, no book page seen): (1) NZ Herald piece citing Stone: Price said hold under a minute; Bezos dialed on speakerphone, 30 executives waited 4.5 min; Bezos said he was only calling to check and hung up. (2) Goodreads reader highlight of the book via search summary: Price assured 'well under a minute' with little proof; 800 number on speakerphone in middle of conference table; hold music. (3) Bezos on Lex Fridman podcast (Dec 2023; Upworthy, IBTimes, UNILAD): wait more than 10 minutes, group waited in silence; the book figure is ~4.5. (4) Stone's Bloomberg Businessweek excerpt (Oct 2013) via nextdraft.com and grimbeorn.blogspot.com: question-mark e-mail = 'ticking bomb', few hours to fix and write thorough explanation, reviewed by succession of managers before reaching Bezos; escalations are Bezos's way of making sure the customer's voice is constantly heard; Jeff Wilke: every customer anecdote matters, each researched because it says something about processes. (5) Empty chair: Bill Price in Hyken interview (hyken.com): 'I was in the very first meeting at Amazon where Jeff left the chair empty'; chair kept empty for the customer because the customer can never come to our meetings. Chair is Price's recollection; Stone's coverage of it only seen in a review summary. Not verified: book page numbers; year; whether chair and speakerphone were the same meeting (story keeps them separate); hold music wording; Wilke's title and who put the question to him (story says only 'asked why'); Price resigned under a year later (secondary only, not used); watch-off detail (not used); 'angrily' (not used).
facts: Bezos asked Bill Price, Amazon's vice president of customer service, for the average phone hold time; Price said well under a minute, with little proof (Stone via reader highlight).
Bezos put the speakerphone in the middle of the conference table and dialed Amazon's 800 number while about 30 executives waited.
In Stone's account about four and a half minutes passed before an agent answered; Bezos said he was only calling to check and hung up.
Years later, on a podcast (2023), Bezos remembered the wait as more than ten minutes and the room silent.
Bezos forwarded customer complaint e-mails to the responsible executive with a single added character, a question mark.
Stone: employees reacted as if they had found a ticking bomb; they had a few hours to solve the issue and prepare a thorough explanation, reviewed by a succession of managers before it reached Bezos.
Stone: such escalations are Bezos's way of making sure the customer's voice is constantly heard inside the company.

Asked why whole teams must drop everything for a question mark, Jeff Wilke answered that every customer anecdote matters and each is researched because it says something about the company's processes.
Price recalled being in the very first meeting where Bezos left a chair empty, for the customer, who can never come to the company's meetings.

Bezos on the Lex Fridman podcast (2023): in a weekly business review a customer-service metric in a deck said wait times were under 60 seconds, but customer complaints suggested otherwise; after the call he said they were not measuring the right thing, which set off a chain of events in which they started measuring it right (Upworthy, UNILAD, IBTimes; not Stone).
Hyken interview: Bezos asked Price in his job interview for his definition of customer service; Price answered that the best service is no service, and Bezos hired him (Price's account, not Stone).
scene_details: a speakerphone in the middle of a conference table
about 30 executives listening to hold music
an empty chair at the table
a forwarded e-mail with only a question mark
tension: Price said hold time was well under a minute; the speakerphone said about four and a half.
opening_idea: Open differently per language: speakerphone, question mark, Price's answer, or the empty chair.

lessons.idea: Give the person who lives with a decision a place in the room, or test the report against their real experience.
lessons.anchor: the empty chair / the speakerphone call

reflect_final: In your next decision, who will live with the result without being in the room, and how would you find out what they would say?

use_cases.situation: A team is about to ship a change.
use_cases.move: Leave one chair empty and ask what the person who will use it would say.
Ask what the child who is not in the room would say.
Write the name of the person affected and one sentence in their voice.

pocket_idea: An empty chair at the table, kept for the person the decision lands on.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Price said under a minute; Bezos dialed and the wait was about four and a half.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Speakerphone call, question-mark e-mails and an empty chair: three ways Bezos put the customer in the room.
